representations.text: During March 30–April 12, RMSSD briefly fell below the 28-day baseline of 44.5 ms (43–47): four consecutive days, April 3–6, measured 22–28 ms, spanning Friday through Monday. It returned to 43–47 ms on April 7 and stayed there through April 12. This episode lowered the window mean to 39.4 ms (−11.6%), without a sustained decline. Resting heart rate remained 55–57 bpm, averaging 56.0 versus 56.1; its window correlation with RMSSD was moderately inverse (r=−0.54), without establishing causation. Sleep stayed near baseline (468.5 versus 470.5 minutes), starting 22:42–22:58 and ending 07:00, with similar weekday/weekend durations. Steps were unchanged (8,061 versus 8,054/day). Active time decreased slightly (53.0 versus 55.4 minutes), especially weekends (50.8 versus 55.6), with activity beginning at 21:00. Low movement remained about 450 versus 448 minutes in interrupted daytime bouts. Activity versus following sleep had only a weak association (r=−0.25; 13 pairs). All observations were complete.

Sleep shifted sharply late in March 30–April 12. Against the 28-day baseline of 470.5 minutes and starts around 22:49, the first eight wake dates recorded 474–485 minutes. April 7–12 then had six consecutive shorter sleeps of 385–392 minutes, about 79–86 minutes below baseline, with starts at 00:08–00:15 and unchanged 07:00 endings. This persisted across weekdays and the final weekend, with no return observed; the window mean was 440.6 minutes (−30). Activity changed from 50–60 minutes beginning at 21:00 to six 90-minute bouts at 20:30–22:00 and eight 45-minute bouts at 17:30–18:15, averaging 64.3 versus 55.6 minutes. Short sleeps followed both schedules; aligned activity/following-sleep correlation was negligible (r=−0.07; 13 pairs). Steps increased modestly (8,088 versus 7,947/day), with fewer weekend than weekday steps (7,906 versus 8,161). Low movement stayed near 449 versus 448 minutes in interrupted bouts. Resting heart rate and RMSSD remained near baseline (56.4 versus 55.9 bpm; 45.7 versus 45.0 ms). All observations were complete.

March 30–April 12 largely maintained the preceding 28-day pattern. Sleep timestamps stayed exactly 01:00–09:00 throughout all 42 days, while recorded sleep averaged 475.1 versus 475.5 minutes, with a window range of 472–479 minutes and essentially no trend. Weekday and weekend sleep remained similar (475.4 and 474.5 minutes). Steps averaged 7,935 versus 7,963/day; they rose modestly within the window (+11.5/day), while weekend steps remained higher than weekdays (8,065 versus 7,883), as in baseline. Active time was stable at 54.4 versus 53.9 minutes, with daily bouts starting at 21:00; low movement averaged 448.9 versus 450.3 minutes in ten daytime bouts separated by five-minute gaps. Resting heart rate averaged 55.9 versus 56.2 bpm, and RMSSD 45.8 versus 45.0 ms, remaining within their baseline ranges. There was no clear steps/activity relationship (r=0.04) or heart-rate/RMSSD relationship (r=0.14). Activity versus following sleep was modestly inverse (r=−0.32; 13 pairs), with little sleep variation and no causal inference. All observations were complete.

Across all 14 days of March 30–April 12, low movement increased to exactly 480 minutes/day from the 28-day baseline mean of 449.3 (+30.8; 6.8%). Its structure changed substantially: baseline had ten 44–47-minute bouts from 10:00 to roughly 18:00, separated by five-minute gaps; the window had 32 separate 15-minute bouts from 10:00–20:35, also with five-minute gaps. Thirty-one gaps contained a recorded one-minute activity bout. This pattern persisted on weekdays and weekends, without return. Total active time nevertheless stayed unchanged (55.3 minutes/day), redistributed from one evening bout to those brief daytime bouts plus 19–28 minutes starting at 21:00. Steps averaged 8,038 versus 8,026/day but declined within the window (slope −29/day). Sleep remained stable (471.1 versus 469.8 minutes), starting 22:42–22:58 and ending 07:00, with similar weekday/weekend durations. Resting heart rate was unchanged at 55.9 bpm; RMSSD averaged 45.6 versus 45.4 ms. Activity/following-sleep association was weak (r=0.25; 13 pairs), as were other supplied relationships. All observations were complete.
